newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark to eye next Fed move if FOMC hikes rates.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark to eye next Fed move if FOMC hikes rates.

text.p: Dollar/mark is discounting a modest snugging of U.S. interest rates by the Federal Reserve on Tuesday, and any retreat after such news should be limited by speculation that more tightening is in the pipeline, currency experts said.

"The critical thing people will shift to ... and I think the bond market is moving in that directon, is that there will be more tightening in the cycle," said David Gilmore, partner at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.

In keeping with a "buy-the-rumor, sell-the-fact" tradition, the dollar is expected to decline after being propped above 1.68 marks since Friday by mounting expectations the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will deliver a 25-basis-point increase in the 5.25 percent federal funds target rate on Tuesday.

"You may get a little bit of a dip for the dollar even if they don't do anything with rates, but I wouldn't expect to get below where we were earlier this year, towards the 1.66 mark area," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.

The most recent survey conducted by Reuters shows 34 of 48 North American economists expect the Fed to raise its funds target to at least 5.50 percent on Tuesday. In the survey a week earlier, only 17 of 44 predicted a rise.
But analysts said the depth of any pullback will hinge on the FOMC's statement, expected at 1415 EST/1915 GMT.

"It depends on how the Fed announces a hike and if the market assumes right away there is going to be another 25 basis points in May, which is also our view," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Chandler said his firm expected a third 25-basis-point hike before the end of 1997.

Other analysts said although they did not expect a replay of the last tightening cycle in 1994 and 1995, when the central bank raised rates a total of seven times, the Fed is unlikely to stand pat after moving once.
Absolute interest rate differentials between the U.S. and Germany may be a less important dollar support than the perception that the U.S. economy continues to outpace Germany's, analysts said.
Spreads might not widen significantly if German market interest rates track U.S. yields higher, as Bundesbank coucil member Ernst Welteke on Monday suggested they might do.
Welteke was quoted by German radio as saying an increase in U.S. rates could push German rates higher, which would not be desirable amid current conditions.

"Until the German data really warrant a shift in the economic outlook in Germany and hence in the interest rate outlook for the Bundesbank, it is still supportive, even though the differentials might not widen much more in favor of the dollar," Gilmore said.
"It's really a function of perceptions. The U.S. economy, on a relative basis, looks quite strong and Germany has got to be facing some significant headwinds from fiscal drag," he said.

"The dollar's relative strength against the deutschemark is just as much (reflecting) concerns about (European Economic and Monetary Union), and the whole economic prospect facing Germany as it is the relatively optimistic picture here in the United States," Finstrom of Smith Barney added.
But Finstrom said the dollar ultimately could take its cue from the reaction of U.S. bonds and stocks to the Fed's decision. She said she did not anticipate a dollar rise above the 1.71 mark area.
Chandler and Gilmore, on the other hand, both looked for new highs for the dollar.
"More hikes ahead are in the cards and that should take us back above 1.72 marks and probably above 1.75," Gilmore said.
